learningObjectives: Explain the physiological or methodological basis of Z-Scores and Effect Sizes.
Apply Z-Scores and Effect Sizes to technically valid clinical interpretation.
Identify artifacts, confounds and limits that could alter conclusions.
Communicate findings without exceeding the evidence or professional scope.

mechanismMap.label: Core concept
mechanismMap.detail: A z-score describes distance from a normative mean in standard-deviation units.

mechanismMap.label: Mechanism
mechanismMap.detail: Extreme values may occur by chance when many channels and metrics are tested. Distribution assumptions, reliability and correction matter.

mechanismMap.label: Clinical integration
mechanismMap.detail: Supports disciplined interpretation of magnitude and uncertainty.

mechanismMap.label: Boundary condition
mechanismMap.detail: Treating |z| > 2 as automatically clinically meaningful inflates false positives.

quizBank.question: Which statement best captures Z-Scores and Effect Sizes?
options: A z-score describes distance from a normative mean in standard-deviation units.
It provides a stand-alone psychiatric diagnosis
It is unaffected by state and artifact
Its interpretation requires no clinical context
quizBank.explanation: A z-score describes distance from a normative mean in standard-deviation units.

quizBank.question: What is the safest clinical principle for Z-Scores and Effect Sizes?
options: Integrate raw signal quality, state, method and clinical context
Assume a coloured map shows exact anatomy
Treat statistical rarity as proof of disorder
quizBank.explanation: EEG and QEEG interpretation requires converging evidence, technical validity and clinical context.

quizBank.question: Which error is most important to avoid in Z-Scores and Effect Sizes?
